title: DNS Enumeration: Reading the Infrastructure Story
content:
Here is the misconception most people carry about DNS:

'DNS converts domain names to IP addresses. That's it.'

It is not 'that's it.' Not even close.

DNS is a public database. It stores multiple types of records about a domain, each designed to serve a specific purpose — and each one revealing something different about the organisation that owns it. DNS enumeration is the practice of systematically querying every record type for a domain and all its subdomains, assembling a complete picture of the target's internet-facing infrastructure from public records alone.

Think of it this way. A large company has a public information directory. Not just a front door address — a full directory with departments listed inside. The A record is the front door address. The MX record is the address of the mail room. The NS record tells you which management office keeps the building's official records. The TXT record is the notice board — full of posted announcements and verification certificates. The CNAME record is a forwarding sign: 'For payroll, please proceed to the annex building on Oak Street.' The PTR record is the reverse directory: look up a phone number to find whose desk it belongs to. The SRV record is the services catalog: which departments offer which professional services, and where to find them.

Every one of these is publicly accessible. Every one of them is queryable by anyone with an internet connection. Every one of them was added by the organisation themselves — because the internet only works if these records exist.

**The A Record: The Front Door Address**

The A record (Address record) maps a domain or subdomain to an IPv4 address. It is the most fundamental DNS record — the one everyone knows. But there is more to it than a single lookup reveals.

**What it is**: A record maps 'meridian-financial.com' to an IPv4 address like '104.22.7.45'. Every time your browser visits a website, it performs an A record lookup for the domain.

**Why it exists**: Computers route traffic by numbers, not names. A records are the translation layer — the published directory listing that says 'this name corresponds to this address.'

**Multiple A records — load balancing and CDN rotation**: A single domain can have multiple A records, each pointing to a different IP. This is how load balancers work: traffic is distributed across multiple servers, each with its own A record. CDNs rotate between different IPs based on where in the world the request comes from. If you query 'google.com' from India, you get a different IP than if you query from Germany — both are correct A records for the same domain.

**What this means for reconnaissance**: The IP in an A record is your starting point, not your conclusion. Always run an IP WHOIS lookup on the returned IP immediately. If it belongs to Cloudflare or a CDN — you are looking at a proxy, not the real server. The real servers are elsewhere.

**Wildcard A records**: Some organisations configure a wildcard record — *.meridian-financial.com — which means any subdomain that has no specific DNS record resolves to a default IP. This is convenient but dangerous from a security perspective: it means every undefined subdomain (including ones that look legitimate but are created by attackers) points somewhere real.

**The AAAA Record: The Same Door, IPv6 Format**

The AAAA record (Quad-A record) maps a domain to an IPv6 address. It does exactly what the A record does — but for IPv6 rather than IPv4.

**What it is**: AAAA records contain IPv6 addresses in the format 2606:4700:20::681c:745. The 'quad-A' name comes from the fact that IPv6 is 128 bits long, which is four times the 32-bit IPv4 address — hence four As.

**Why it exists**: IPv4 addresses are exhausted. There are only 4.3 billion possible IPv4 addresses and there are far more than 4.3 billion internet-connected devices. IPv6 solves this by providing 340 undecillion addresses — enough for every grain of sand on earth to have its own IP address.

**Reconnaissance significance**: Many organisations have both A and AAAA records for the same domain. The IPv6 infrastructure is frequently less well-monitored, less protected, and sometimes reveals IP ranges that are not visible through IPv4 investigation. A target that has a robust CDN protecting their IPv4 presence sometimes has their IPv6 infrastructure connecting directly to origin servers — because the CDN was configured for IPv4 only. Always query both.

callouts.title: The Eight DNS Record Types You Need to Know
callouts.text:
A — Maps domain to IPv4 address (the web server address)
AAAA — Maps domain to IPv6 address (same purpose, newer format)
MX — Specifies mail exchange servers (reveals email provider)
NS — Specifies authoritative nameservers (reveals DNS host)
TXT — Text records: email policies, service verification (reveals cloud tools)
CNAME — Alias to another domain (reveals CDN and SaaS relationships)
PTR — Reverse DNS: IP address to hostname (the reverse directory)
SRV — Service locator: which server handles which service (intro only)

Each type exists because a different part of the internet needed a place to publish a specific kind of addressing information. Each one reveals something different about the organisation that owns it.

callouts.title: DNS Enumeration vs Port Scanning
callouts.text:
DNS enumeration and port scanning are completely different phases of reconnaissance. DNS enumeration is passive: you are reading public records. No traffic reaches the target's servers. No logs are created on their systems.

Port scanning (Nmap and similar tools) is active: you are sending packets directly to the target's systems. Every port scan creates log entries. Port scanning requires written authorisation.

DNS enumeration always comes first. It tells you WHAT to scan before you begin scanning. A penetration tester who port scans everything without first doing DNS enumeration is wasting time and making noise.

keyTerms.definition: The systematic querying of all available DNS record types for a domain and its subdomains, to build a complete picture of the target's internet-facing infrastructure. Passive by definition — all queries go to public DNS servers, not the target's own systems.

Address record. Maps a domain or subdomain to an IPv4 address. The most fundamental DNS record. Always follow with an IP WHOIS lookup to determine whether the IP belongs to the target or a CDN/cloud provider.

Quad-A record. Maps a domain or subdomain to an IPv6 address. Same purpose as A record, different address format. IPv6 infrastructure is often less protected than IPv4 and may bypass CDN coverage that only covers IPv4 traffic.
